questions.stem: John works in a cake shop. He records which of the five most popular cakes each customer buys. What type of data is this?
questions.hint: Ask: are the categories names with no natural order, or numbers?

steps.explain: The data records a cake *name* (a category), not a number, so it is categorical rather than quantitative.
The five cake types have no natural ranking or order (e.g. "chocolate" is not "more" or "less" than "vanilla"), so it is nominal rather than ordinal.

questions.stem: The Pareto chart below shows the number of orders received each month (bars) and the cumulative percentage of orders (line). What percentage of orders were received in May?
questions.hint: May's own share is the *difference* between the cumulative % up to May and the cumulative % up to April.

steps.explain: The cumulative % line reaches 50% after April and 70% after May, so May alone contributed the gap between these two readings.
Checking directly from the bar heights confirms this: May had 9 orders out of \(25+9+7.5+5+2.5=49\) total orders.
The bar-height calculation is the precise one — May accounts for 18% of total orders.

questions.stem: A sample of 14 people were asked how many hours of television they watched the previous night. The results are shown in the dot plot below. Find the mean and sample standard deviation of these times, correct to one decimal place.

steps.explain: Read the frequencies directly from the dot plot: \(x=0\) has 3 dots, \(x=1\) has 2, \(x=2\) has 4, \(x=3\) has 2, \(x=4\) has 2, \(x=5\) has 1 (total \(3+2+4+2+2+1=14\), matching the sample size).
Convert each frequency to a probability (proportion) by dividing by 14, then compute the mean \(\bar x = \sum x\cdot p\).
Evaluate the sum.
For the sample standard deviation, first find \(E(X^2)\), then use \(s = \sqrt{E(X^2)-\bar x^2}\) (using calculator statistics mode for the sample SD directly is equally valid).
Substitute into the standard deviation formula and evaluate.
State both final answers, rounded to 1 decimal place.

questions.stem: Which statement is true for an ungrouped data set with no outliers?
options: The largest possible range is 5 times the interquartile range.
The largest possible range is 3 times the interquartile range.
The largest possible range is 4 times the interquartile range.
The largest possible range is 2 times the interquartile range.
questions.hint: A value is an outlier if it lies more than \(1.5 \times \text{IQR}\) beyond \(Q_1\) or \(Q_3\) — with no outliers, the most extreme values sit right at that boundary.

steps.explain: With no outliers, the minimum and maximum values can each be at most \(1.5\,\text{IQR}\) away from \(Q_1\) and \(Q_3\) respectively (any further and they would be outliers).
The range spans from the minimum to the maximum, which is the IQR itself plus the two 1.5-IQR margins on either side.
Add the three portions together.

questions.stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between expenditure per primary school student (as a % of GDP) and life expectancy (years) for 15 countries. The lower quartile of expenditure is \(Q_L=8.4\) and upper quartile \(Q_U=22.5\).

parts.stem: (a) What is the interquartile range for the expenditure data?

steps.explain: Subtract the lower quartile from the upper quartile.
Evaluate.

parts.stem: (b) Another country has an expenditure of 47.6% of GDP. Would this country be an outlier for this data set?
options: No, since 47.6 is close to the other high values
parts.hint: A value is an outlier if it lies beyond \(Q_U+1.5\times\text{IQR}\) (or below \(Q_L-1.5\times\text{IQR}\)).

steps.explain: Calculate the outlier boundary above \(Q_U\), using the IQR found in part (a).
Compare the new country's value to this boundary.
Since the value exceeds the outlier boundary, it is classified as an outlier.

parts.stem: (d) Using the least-squares line \(y=1.29x+49.9\), estimate the life expectancy in a country with an expenditure of 18% of GDP.
parts.hint: Substitute \(x=18\) into the given regression line.

steps.explain: Substitute \(x=18\) into the regression equation.
Evaluate.
Round appropriately (reading directly from the graph, values between 72-74 are all acceptable).

parts.stem: (e) Why is this line NOT useful for predicting life expectancy in a country with an expenditure of 60% of its GDP?

steps.explain: Substitute \(x=60\) into the regression line to see what it predicts.
This predicted life expectancy (over 100 years) far exceeds any realistic human life expectancy, and 60% of GDP is well outside the range of the original data (5%-27.5%).
steps.work: Predicted \(y>100\), unrealistic; \(x=60\) is outside the observed data range

steps.explain: This is extrapolation — using the line far beyond the range it was fitted to — which is not a reliable prediction method.
steps.work: \(\therefore\) the line is only reliable (predictive) within the range of the original data, not for extrapolated values like 60% GDP.

questions.stem: Sets of data on the attention span of participants (in seconds) are collected for two groups of people. The stem-and-leaf plot shows the data for Group X. Using the same scale as the given box plot for Group A, draw a box plot for Group X.

steps.explain: List the 15 values for Group X in order from the stem-and-leaf plot, then find the five-number summary (minimum, \(Q_1\), median, \(Q_3\), maximum).
With \(n=15\) values, the median is the 8th value. \(Q_1\) is the median of the lower 7 values, \(Q_3\) is the median of the upper 7 values.
Draw the box plot using this five-number summary, aligned to the same number-line scale as Group A shown above.

steps.explain: Repeat the same comparison for Group X.

steps.work: \(\text{lower whisker} = 31-23=8 > \text{upper whisker} = 47-44=3 \implies \text{Group X is strongly negatively (left) skewed}\)

steps.work: \(\text{Group X is MORE negatively skewed than Group A}\)

questions.stem: A biologist measured the amount of fertiliser (\(x\), grams) given to 8 tomato plants and the resulting yield (\(y\), kg). The scatterplot below shows the 8 data points with a fitted line, and \(R^2 = 0.9453\).

parts.stem: (a) Describe the association between yield and fertiliser in terms of strength and direction.
parts.hint: Look at how tightly the points cluster around the line, and whether \(y\) increases or decreases as \(x\) increases.

steps.explain: As fertiliser increases, yield also increases — a positive association. The points sit very close to a straight line, and \(R^2=0.9453\) is close to 1, confirming a strong linear relationship.

parts.stem: (b) Determine the equation of the least-squares regression line, rounding values to 2 significant figures.
parts.hint: Use linear regression (by calculator statistics mode, or estimate the gradient and intercept from two well-spaced points on the fitted line).

steps.explain: Using calculator statistics (linear regression) mode on the 8 data pairs gives the slope and intercept directly.
Round each value to 2 significant figures.

parts.stem: (c) A plant with 2.2 grams of fertiliser was not recorded. Use the regression line from part (b) to predict its yield.
parts.hint: Substitute \(x=2.2\) into the regression equation from part (b).

steps.explain: Substitute \(x=2.2\) into the regression line \(y=1.4x+2.6\).
Evaluate.

parts.stem: (d) Explain why you should not extrapolate from this data to predict the yield for high rates of fertiliser usage.

steps.explain: The regression line is only reliable within the range of \(x\)-values that were actually tested (from 1.0 g to 3.5 g).

Outside this range, there could be a point where extra fertiliser no longer produces extra yield — e.g. too much fertiliser can damage the plant, or other factors (sunlight, water) may limit yield regardless of fertiliser rate.
steps.work: The linear trend may not continue — extrapolation assumes a relationship that was never actually observed.

questions.stem: A scatterplot of reported pain against drug dosage (mg) is shown below. How could you describe the correlation between the pain and the dosage?
questions.hint: As dosage increases, does pain tend to increase or decrease? How tightly do the points cluster around a line?

steps.explain: As the dosage increases along the \(x\)-axis, the reported pain generally decreases — this is a negative (downward) trend.
The points do not sit tightly on a line, but they do show a fairly consistent downward pattern — not strong, but more than weak.
steps.work: Strength: moderate scatter around the trend

steps.explain: Combine strength and direction.

questions.stem: The graph shows a scatterplot for a set of data. Which of the following values is the most appropriate Pearson's correlation coefficient for this data?
questions.hint: The points trend downward but do not sit tightly on a straight line — a value between 0 and \(-1\), moderately strong, is appropriate.

steps.explain: As \(x\) increases, \(y\) tends to decrease — the trend is negative, ruling out any positive value.
The points show a fairly consistent downward pattern but with some scatter — not perfectly linear (which would be exactly \(-1\)), but stronger than a weak correlation like \(-0.35\).
The value that best matches "negative, moderately strong" is \(-0.63\).

Figtree Syndrome is a rare disease. The table shows research spending (% of GDP) $x$ and cases of Figtree Syndrome (1000s) $y$ for 10 countries.

| $x$ | 2.0 | 2.4 | 3.0 | 3.2 | 3.5 | 3.8 | 4.1 | 4.5 | 4.6 | 5.0 |

parts.stem: Find the least squares regression line for this data. Round your values to 3 significant figures.

steps.explain: Assuming you still have the data entered from Q17(a) in your Casio fx-82AU PLUS calculator. (If not, press **MODE** $\rightarrow$ **2 (STAT)** $\rightarrow$ **2 (A+BX)**, enter the $x$ and $y$ values, and press **AC**).

To find the $y$-intercept ($a$) of the least squares regression line $\hat{y} = a + bx$:

1. Press **SHIFT** and then **1 (STAT)**.
2. Select **5 (Reg)**.
3. Select **1 (A)**.
4. Press **=** to calculate.

Rounding to 3 significant figures, $a \approx 10.4$.

To find the slope ($b$) of the regression line:

1. Press **SHIFT** and then **1 (STAT)**.
2. Select **5 (Reg)**.
3. Select **2 (B)**.
4. Press **=** to calculate.

Rounding to 3 significant figures, $b \approx -1.28$.
Construct the final regression equation by substituting your calculated $a$ and $b$ into the formula $\hat{y} = a + bx$.

questions.hint: Use your calculator's linear regression function to find the slope $b$ and intercept $a$ of $\hat{y} = a + bx$.
questions.solution: Using the calculator: slope $b \approx -1.28$, intercept $a \approx 10.4$. Regression line: $\hat{y} = -1.28x + 10.4$.

questions.stem: Max surveyed a group of people about their age and weekly wage. \\ \(\begin{array}{c|cccccc} \text{Age (years)}\ x & 18 & 45 & 28 & 15 & 32 & 68 \\ \hline \text{Wage (\$/week)}\ W & 715 & 2350 & 1530 & 438 & 1690 & 1320 \end{array}\)

parts.stem: (a) Find the correlation coefficient \( r \), and classify the type and strength of correlation.

steps.explain: Using a Casio fx-82AU PLUS II calculator, first set it to Statistical Linear Regression mode by pressing **[MODE] → [2] (STAT) → [2] (A+BX)**.
Enter the data into the X (Age) and Y (Wage) columns, pressing **[=]** after each value. Once all 6 pairs are entered, press **[AC]** to clear the screen (the data is safely saved).
To find the correlation coefficient \( r \), press **[SHIFT] → [1] (STAT) → [5] (Reg) → [3] (r) → [=]**.
Since \( r \approx 0.53 \) is between 0.5 and 0.7, it represents a moderate positive correlation (wage tends to increase moderately with age).

parts.stem: (b) Find the equation of the least-squares regression line in the form \( W=Bx+A \), where \( A \) and \( B \) are integers.

steps.explain: Continuing with the saved data on your calculator, you can find the regression coefficients \( A \) (y-intercept) and \( B \) (gradient).
Find the y-intercept \( A \) by pressing **[SHIFT] → [1] (STAT) → [5] (Reg) → [1] (A) → [=]**.
Find the gradient \( B \) by pressing **[SHIFT] → [1] (STAT) → [5] (Reg) → [2] (B) → [=]**.
Round both values to the nearest integer as required (A = 706, B = 18) and substitute them into the regression equation \( W = Bx + A \).

parts.stem: (c) Use the equation from part (b) to estimate the earnings of a 50-year-old worker.

steps.explain: Substitute \( x=50 \) into the regression equation \( W=18x+706 \) found in part (b).
Evaluate the multiplication, then add.
State the estimated weekly wage.

parts.stem: (d) Could your equation from part (b) be used to make valid estimates for ages greater than 68 and less than 15 years? Validate your response with calculations and/or reasons.
parts.answer: No — extrapolating beyond the sample's age range (15 to 68 years) is unreliable, since there is no data confirming the linear trend continues outside that range.

steps.explain: The regression line was fitted using only the six data points, whose ages range from the youngest (15) to the oldest (68) in the sample.

Using the equation to predict outcomes for \( x \)-values outside this range is called extrapolation. There is no evidence that the same linear trend continues beyond the range that was actually observed — the relationship could level off, reverse, or become non-linear (e.g. wages typically don't keep rising indefinitely with age, especially near or after retirement).

Note that a moderate correlation coefficient (from part (a)) describes the strength of the relationship WITHIN the observed data — it says nothing about whether that relationship still holds outside the sampled range.

Part (a): using the six data pairs (age, wage) — (18,715), (45,2350), (28,1530), (15,438), (32,1690), (68,1320) — compute the correlation coefficient r using the standard formula (or calculator statistics mode).
steps.work: \(r = \dfrac{n\sum xy - \sum x \sum y}{\sqrt{\left[n\sum x^2-(\sum x)^2\right]\left[n\sum y^2-(\sum y)^2\right]}}\)\\ Evaluating with the six data points gives \(r \approx 0.87\).

steps.explain: Interpret the value of r.
steps.work: Since \(r \approx 0.87\) is close to 1 and positive, this indicates a strong, positive linear correlation between age and wage.

steps.explain: Part (b): find the least-squares regression line \(W = Bx + A\) using the standard formulas \(B=\dfrac{n\sum xy-\sum x\sum y}{n\sum x^2-(\sum x)^2}\) and \(A=\bar{y}-B\bar{x}\) (or calculator regression mode).
steps.work: Using the six data points: \(B \approx 31.5\), \(A \approx -15.4\)\\ So the regression line is \(W \approx 31.5x - 15.4\)

steps.explain: Part (c): substitute \(x=50\) into the regression equation to estimate the wage of a 50-year-old.
Part (d): assess whether the regression equation can be validly used outside the range of the original data (ages 15 to 68).
steps.work: No. Using the equation for ages below 15 or above 68 requires extrapolation beyond the range of the collected data. The linear trend observed within \([15,68]\) is not guaranteed to continue outside this range (e.g. wages typically decline near/after retirement age, and there is no data to confirm the relationship holds for children), so predictions outside this range are not reliable.

questions.stem: The table gives the amount withdrawn (\(x\), dollars) and the time until the next withdrawal (\(y\), hours) at an ATM for 10 transactions:

parts.stem: (a) Find the least-squares regression line \( y=A+Bx \), and use it to estimate the withdrawal amount (to the nearest $10) when the time until the next withdrawal is 120 hours.

steps.explain: Press \(\text{MODE}\), then select \(\text{STAT}\) (option 2), then select \(\text{2: A+BX}\) for linear regression. A two-column table (X, Y) appears.
Type each X-value then press \(=\) to move to the Y column, type the matching Y-value, then press \(=\) again to move to the next row. Repeat for all 10 withdrawal pairs from the table.

Once all 10 pairs are entered, press \(\text{AC}\) to leave the table (the data stays stored). Then press \(\text{SHIFT}\;1\) to open the STAT menu, select \(\text{5: Reg}\), then \(\text{1: A}\) to read off the intercept.
Press \(\text{SHIFT}\;1\) again, select \(\text{5: Reg}\), then \(\text{2: B}\) to read off the gradient. Together, \(A\) and \(B\) give the regression equation \(y=A+Bx\).
Substitute \(y=120\) into the regression equation and solve for \(x\) (withdrawal amount).

Round to the nearest \(\$10\). Pitfall: mixing up which variable is the response (\(y\)) and which is the predictor (\(x\)) when solving swaps the roles of \(A\) and \(B\), as in the second distractor.

parts.stem: (b) Find the correlation coefficient \( r \) and describe the nature of the relationship.

steps.explain: The data is already stored in two-variable statistics mode from part (a) — no need to re-enter it. Press \(\text{SHIFT}\;1\) to open the STAT menu, then select \(\text{5: Reg}\).
From the Reg submenu, select \(\text{3: r}\) to read off the correlation coefficient directly.
Since \(r\) is positive, larger withdrawal amounts are associated with longer waits until the next withdrawal.

Since \(|r|\) is close to \(1\) (well above \(0.7\)), classify the strength. Pitfall: reading the sign of \(r\) incorrectly off the calculator display gives the negative-correlation distractor — double-check the displayed sign before rounding.

questions.stem: Hayden is studying the growth of a tree. Heights recorded (metres) at years 1–9 since planting are: \(0.7, 1.4, 2.4, 3.5, H, 6.6, 7.9, 8.7, 9.5\) (year 5's height, \(H\), was not recorded). A scatterplot of the recorded data is shown.

parts.stem: (a) What is Pearson's correlation coefficient (using the 8 recorded points), correct to 4 decimal places?
parts.hint: Use calculator statistics (linear regression) mode on the 8 recorded \((t,h)\) pairs to compute \(r\) directly.

steps.explain: On the fx-82 (Casio), enter Statistics mode and choose linear regression: press MODE, then select STAT, then select the "A+Bx" (linear regression) option.

A table with X and Y columns appears. Enter the 8 RECORDED \((t,h)\) pairs — skip year 5, since \(H\) wasn't recorded. Type each X value, press \(=\), type the matching Y value, press \(=\), and move to the next row.
Once all 8 pairs are entered, press AC to leave the data table and return to the calculation screen.
Open the regression-statistics menu: press SHIFT then 1 (STAT), then select 5 (Reg) from the menu that appears.
The Reg menu lists \(A\), \(B\), and \(r\). Select \(r\) (Pearson's correlation coefficient) and press \(=\) to display its value.
Round to 4 decimal places.

parts.stem: (b) Find the equation of the least-squares line of best fit in terms of years (\(t\)) and height (\(h\)), correct to 2 decimal places.
parts.hint: Use calculator statistics (linear regression) mode on the 8 recorded pairs to find the slope and intercept directly.

steps.explain: The 8 data pairs are still stored from part (a) (no need to re-enter them). Reopen the regression menu: SHIFT 1 (STAT) → 5 (Reg).
This time select \(B\) (the gradient) and press \(=\).
Reopen the same Reg menu (SHIFT 1 → 5) and select \(A\) (the \(y\)-intercept) and press \(=\).
Write the regression equation in the form \(h=Bt+A\), rounding each coefficient to 2 decimal places.

parts.stem: (c) Predict the height, \(H\), after 5 years, correct to one decimal place.
parts.hint: Substitute \(t=5\) into the regression line from part (b).

steps.explain: Substitute \(t=5\) into the regression equation found in part (b).
Evaluate on the calculator (a plain arithmetic calculation — no STAT mode needed here) and round to 1 decimal place.

questions.stem: A manager is in charge of four teenage employees. The number of weeks they have been working (\(x\)) and the number of times they ask for assistance during a four-hour shift (\(y\)) are: \((2,15), (6,10), (10,6), (17,3)\). Use a calculator to find the equation of the least-squares regression line for this dataset, finding the gradient and \(y\)-intercept to 2 decimal places.

steps.explain: On your calculator, enter the four data points into two-variable (bivariate) statistics mode, then request the linear regression coefficients.
Reading the gradient (\(b\)) and \(y\)-intercept (\(a\)) from the calculator's regression output, rounded to 2 decimal places.
Write the full equation of the regression line.

questions.stem: Using the least-squares regression line \(y=-0.79x+15.38\) as a guide, on average how many full weeks will an employee have been working before they require assistance less than 8 times during a four-hour shift?

steps.explain: Find the value of \(x\) where the regression line predicts exactly \(y=8\), by substituting and solving.
Rearrange to solve for \(x\).

Since the gradient is negative (\(y\) decreases as \(x\) increases), assistance requests drop below 8 only once \(x\) exceeds \(9.34\) weeks. Check the next WHOLE (full) week: at \(x=9\), \(y\approx 15.38-0.79(9)=8.27>8\) still, but at \(x=10\), \(y\approx 15.38-0.79(10)=7.48<8\).
The first full week where the prediction drops below 8 is week 10.
